source: Submarine Force Museum: exhibits as described by visitors and Wikipedia; pictures from Wikimedia Commons; the Nautilus tour compartments

artworks.title: USS Nautilus (SSN-571)
artworks.description: The world’s first nuclear-powered submarine. President Truman laid her keel at Electric Boat, across the river, in 1952, and Mamie Eisenhower christened her in January 1954. On January 17, 1955 she signalled “Underway on nuclear power”. On August 3, 1958 she was the first ship to reach the North Pole, passing under the Arctic ice (Operation Sunshine). Decommissioned in 1980, she has been a museum ship here since 1986: 97 m (319 ft) long.
artworks.galleryName: Historic Ship Nautilus (SSN-571), the first nuclear-powered submarine: a self-guided audio tour of the forward compartments, about 30 minutes (see the Nautilus floor)

artworks.title: Forward Torpedo Room
artworks.description: Where the tour begins, at the foot of the ladder from the deckhouse: the breech doors of the six bow torpedo tubes, the reload racks, and crew bunks tucked in between the torpedoes.
artworks.galleryName: Forward Torpedo Room: six torpedo tubes, reload racks and bunks squeezed between them

artworks.title: Crew’s berthing and chiefs’ quarters
artworks.description: Bunks three high, each with a thin mattress, a reading light and a small locker: this was home for months at a time. Life-size mannequins show the crew at work and at rest throughout the boat.
artworks.galleryName: Crew’s berthing and the chiefs’ quarters: three-high bunks

artworks.title: Galley
artworks.description: A kitchen the size of a closet, where the cooks baked bread and made four meals a day for a crew of about 100. Good food was the submariner’s great comfort.
artworks.galleryName: Galley, where four cooks fed more than 100 men

artworks.title: Crew’s mess
artworks.description: The crew’s dining room was also their classroom, cinema and meeting room. Nautilus was one of the first submarines with an ice cream machine, a jukebox and a library.
artworks.galleryName: Crew’s mess: meals, movies, training and meetings; the battery well under a glass hatch in the deck

artworks.title: Battery well
artworks.description: Seen through a glass hatch in the deck: the batteries kept for emergencies, if the reactor shut down.
artworks.galleryName: Crew’s mess: meals, movies, training and meetings; the battery well under a glass hatch in the deck

artworks.title: Emergency Air Breathing masks
artworks.description: Masks on hoses that plug into air manifolds all through the boat, so the crew could breathe in a fire or a smoke-filled compartment.
artworks.galleryName: Crew’s berthing and the chiefs’ quarters: three-high bunks
artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say where this is shown: our guess by subject.

artworks.title: Attack center
artworks.description: The heart of the boat: the periscopes, the fire-control equipment and a mannequin of the Officer of the Deck at the periscope. A voice tube passed orders down to the control room.
artworks.galleryName: Attack Center: periscopes, fire control and the Officer of the Deck; a voice tube passes orders to the control room below

artworks.title: Control room
artworks.description: The diving and steering stations, where the planesmen and helmsman drove the boat on the orders sent down from the attack center above.
artworks.galleryName: Control room: the diving and steering stations, under the attack center
artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say where this is shown: our guess by subject.

artworks.title: Wardroom
artworks.description: The officers’ dining room, also their office and meeting room. Here the crew planned the 1958 voyage under the North Pole.
artworks.galleryName: Wardroom, the officers’ dining and meeting room

artworks.title: Captain’s and Executive Officer’s staterooms
artworks.description: The only private cabins on board, each barely bigger than a bunk and a desk. Commander William R. Anderson slept here on the North Pole voyage.
artworks.galleryName: Officers’ country: the Captain’s and Executive Officer’s staterooms and the small arms locker

artworks.title: Small arms locker
artworks.description: Shotguns and rifles kept for the watch on deck when the submarine was in port.
artworks.galleryName: Officers’ country: the Captain’s and Executive Officer’s staterooms and the small arms locker
artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say where this is shown: our guess by subject.

artworks.title: Reactor and engine rooms
artworks.description: The S2W reactor, built by Westinghouse under Admiral Hyman Rickover’s Naval Reactors program, and the steam turbines it drove are aft of the tour, and closed to visitors.
artworks.galleryName: Reactor compartment and engine rooms: not open to visitors (the tour stops here and goes back up to the deckhouse)

artworks.title: Sail of USS George Washington (SSBN-598)
artworks.description: The first ballistic-missile submarine, built in Groton and commissioned in 1959, carried 16 Polaris missiles. Strictly, the sail is that of USS Abraham Lincoln: George Washington’s own was replaced after she collided with the Japanese freighter Nissho Maru in 1981.
artworks.galleryName: Memorial Plaza: the sail of USS George Washington (SSBN-598), the Nautilus propellers and the 41 for Freedom memorial

artworks.title: USS Nautilus propellers
artworks.description: Two of the Nautilus’s propellers, taken off when she became a museum ship.
artworks.galleryName: Memorial Plaza: the sail of USS George Washington (SSBN-598), the Nautilus propellers and the 41 for Freedom memorial

artworks.title: 41 for Freedom memorial
artworks.description: A stone memorial to the “41 for Freedom”, the 41 Polaris ballistic-missile submarines built from 1959 to 1967, all named for Americans who stood for freedom, starting with the George Washington.
artworks.galleryName: Memorial Plaza: the sail of USS George Washington (SSBN-598), the Nautilus propellers and the 41 for Freedom memorial

artworks.title: UGM-84 Harpoon missile
artworks.description: Developed in the 1970s as an anti-ship missile, the Harpoon was adapted in the early 1980s to be fired from submarines’ torpedo tubes in a capsule that pops it out of the water. By the museum entrance.
artworks.galleryName: Front lawn: the Japanese HA-8 and the U.S. X-1 midget submarines, a swimmer delivery vehicle, sections of the NR-1, a deck gun and the Harpoon missile at the door

artworks.title: Hull rings: Holland and Ohio
artworks.description: Two steel rings over the walk to the door show how big submarines have grown: the small one is as wide as USS Holland (1900), the Navy’s first submarine; the huge one as wide as an Ohio-class missile submarine.
artworks.galleryName: Walk to the main entrance, under the two hull rings

artworks.title: X-1 midget submarine
artworks.description: The U.S. Navy’s only midget submarine, built in 1955 for four men to test harbour defences. A hydrogen-peroxide explosion blew off her bow in 1957; she was rebuilt and used for research until 1973. 15 m long.
artworks.galleryName: Front lawn: the Japanese HA-8 and the U.S. X-1 midget submarines, a swimmer delivery vehicle, sections of the NR-1, a deck gun and the Harpoon missile at the door

artworks.title: HA-8, Japanese Type A midget submarine
artworks.description: A two-man Ko-hyoteki midget submarine carrying two torpedoes, of the kind used at Pearl Harbor. HA-8 was found at Guadalcanal in World War II and brought to the United States. 24 m long.
artworks.imageCredit: Carol M. Highsmith, PD-Highsmith, via Wikimedia Commons
artworks.galleryName: Front lawn: the Japanese HA-8 and the U.S. X-1 midget submarines, a swimmer delivery vehicle, sections of the NR-1, a deck gun and the Harpoon missile at the door

artworks.title: Swimmer Delivery Vehicle Mk IX
artworks.description: A flooded mini-submersible that carried two scuba-equipped Navy SEALs on secret missions; retired in 1995.
artworks.galleryName: Front lawn: the Japanese HA-8 and the U.S. X-1 midget submarines, a swimmer delivery vehicle, sections of the NR-1, a deck gun and the Harpoon missile at the door

artworks.title: NR-1 deep submergence vessel (sections)
artworks.description: The Navy’s only nuclear-powered deep-sea research submarine, in service for 39 years (1969–2008): it had wheels to drive on the sea floor and helped find the wreck of the space shuttle Challenger. Its exhibit was dedicated in 2015.
artworks.imageCredit: Official U.S. Navy Page from United States of America, CC-PD-Mark, via Wikimedia Commons
artworks.galleryName: Front lawn: the Japanese HA-8 and the U.S. X-1 midget submarines, a swimmer delivery vehicle, sections of the NR-1, a deck gun and the Harpoon missile at the door
artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say where this is shown: our guess by subject.

artworks.title: Submarine deck gun
artworks.description: World War II submarines carried a deck gun to finish off small ships on the surface and save torpedoes.
artworks.galleryName: Front lawn: the Japanese HA-8 and the U.S. X-1 midget submarines, a swimmer delivery vehicle, sections of the NR-1, a deck gun and the Harpoon missile at the door
artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say where this is shown: our guess by subject.

artworks.title: Model of Jules Verne’s Nautilus
artworks.description: Hanging just inside the doors: Captain Nemo’s Nautilus from Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas (1870), the novel that gave the first nuclear submarine its name.
artworks.galleryName: Lobby: the docent desk (free scavenger hunt for children), restrooms, and Jules Verne’s Nautilus hanging just inside the doors
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: Cutaway model of a modern submarine
artworks.description: An interactive model cut open to show the inside of a modern attack submarine, compartment by compartment.
artworks.galleryName: Main Hallway: the cutaway model of a modern submarine and the wall of submarine models, all to one scale, from the Holland to the Columbia class
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: The model wall
artworks.description: Models of U.S. submarines, all at the same scale, in order: from the little Holland of 1900 to the coming Columbia class.
artworks.galleryName: Main Hallway: the cutaway model of a modern submarine and the wall of submarine models, all to one scale, from the Holland to the Columbia class

artworks.title: Control center of USS Sturgeon (SSN-637)
artworks.description: The real control room of a Cold War attack submarine, where you can sit at the controls and try steering.
artworks.galleryName: Control Room: the real control center of USS Sturgeon (SSN-637); take the controls and try steering a submarine
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: Working periscopes
artworks.description: Three periscopes rise through the roof: turn them to see the Nautilus at her pier, the Thames River and the Coast Guard Academy on the far bank.
artworks.galleryName: Attack Center: three working periscopes through the roof; look at the Nautilus, the Thames and the Coast Guard Academy across the river
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: Bushnell’s Turtle (full-size replica)
artworks.description: The first submarine used in war, invented by David Bushnell of Saybrook, Connecticut. In 1776 Sergeant Ezra Lee cranked it by hand under New York harbour to fix a bomb to HMS Eagle; the screw would not bite and he escaped. The replica is cut open to show the one-man cockpit.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: USS Gato model (1/6 scale cutaway)
artworks.description: A model about 15 m (50 ft) long of a World War II fleet submarine, opened up so you can look into every room. Gato-class boats, many built in Groton, fought the Pacific war.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: McCann Submarine Rescue Chamber
artworks.description: A diving bell lowered to a sunken submarine’s escape hatch. In 1939 one like it brought up the 33 survivors of USS Squalus off New Hampshire, the first rescue of its kind.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: Polaris A3 missile
artworks.description: The submarine-launched ballistic missile of the 1960s: 9.8 m (32.3 ft) long and 137 cm (54 in) wide, fired from under water. The 41 for Freedom submarines carried 16 each.
artworks.imageCredit: Kevin King, CC-BY-2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: Italian manned torpedo (SSB “Maiale”)
artworks.description: A torpedo ridden by two divers in breathing sets, who steered it into enemy harbours to fix its warhead under a ship. Italian “pigs” sank two British battleships at Alexandria in 1941; this SSB is the later type.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force
artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say where this is shown: our guess by subject.

artworks.title: Torpedoes
artworks.description: A row of submarine torpedoes from World War II to the Cold War, from the troubled Mark 14 to modern wire-guided weapons.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force
artworks.placeNote: Approximate: no floor plan is published, so this room’s place on the map is our reading.

artworks.title: Bell of USS S-51
artworks.description: S-51 sank off Block Island in 1925 after a collision with the steamer City of Rome; 33 men were lost and 3 survived. Raising her led the Navy to new rescue gear.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force
artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say where this is shown: our guess by subject.

artworks.title: Commissioning bottle of USS Thresher (SSN-593)
artworks.description: Thresher was lost with all 129 men on board during deep-diving tests off New England on April 10, 1963. Her loss led to the SUBSAFE program that has kept U.S. submarines safe since.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force

artworks.title: World War II submarine battle flag
artworks.description: Submarines sewed battle flags with a symbol for every ship they sank: a record of a boat’s war patrols.
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force

artworks.description: A heavy brass diving helmet; scan the QR code beside it to see yourself inside one (augmented reality).
artworks.galleryName: Main Gallery (two storeys high): Bushnell’s Turtle, the big Gato model, the McCann rescue chamber, torpedoes, the Polaris missile and the history of the U.S. Submarine Force

artworks.description: Displays on modern submarines (the Virginia, Ohio and coming Columbia classes, many built across the river at Electric Boat), what submarines do today and how the Submarine Force is commanded.
